nodes.label: Patrick Wolfe
nodes.date_label: Settler Colonialism and the Transformation of Anthropology 1999 · later essays 2001, 2006 · coverage through 2000
nodes.description: Reads the history of anthropology through settler colonialism. Settler Colonialism and the Transformation of Anthropology (1999) studies virgin birth in anthropology and in Australian settler discourse, and Victorian anthropology on mother-right, totemism and E. B. Tylor. Later essays address land, labour and race (2001) and the elimination of the native (2006).
nodes.representative_figures_and_works: Patrick Wolfe (1949–2016); Settler Colonialism and the Transformation of Anthropology: The Politics and Poetics of an Ethnographic Event (1999). Later readings: “Land, Labor, and Difference: Elementary Structures of Race” (2001); “Settler Colonialism and the Elimination of the Native” (2006).
nodes.scope_note: This entry presents the 1999 book. Its introduction (pp. 1–2, read) distinguishes settler from franchise colonies, holds that settler colonies 'were (are) premised on the elimination of native societies' and states that 'invasion is a structure not an event'; the rest of the book is checked at contents and catalogue level. The 2001 and 2006 essays are later readings. He did not originate the term, which has earlier usage (Veracini 2013), and he is not presented as the field's founder.

nodes.label: Ian McKay
nodes.date_label: Tartanism Triumphant 1992 · The Quest of the Folk 1994 · 'A Note on Region' and the liberal order prospectus 2000 · later readings 2005, 2008, 2009 · coverage through 2000
nodes.description: Reads twentieth-century Nova Scotia's 'folk' as a cultural selection by folklorists, handicraft planners, writers and the tourist state, and as a local version of an international antimodernist wave (1992, 1994). In 2000 he proposed treating Canada as a project of liberal rule, to be studied through the implantation of liberalism across a heterogeneous terrain, and asked how 'region' fits that project. Later work turns to the Canadian left as a counter-project (2005, 2008) and answers the framework's critics (2009).
nodes.representative_figures_and_works: Ian McKay (b. 1953); “Tartanism Triumphant: The Construction of Scottishness in Nova Scotia, 1933–1954” (1992); The Quest of the Folk: Antimodernism and Cultural Selection in Twentieth-Century Nova Scotia (1994); “A Note on ‘Region’ in Writing the History of Atlantic Canada” (2000); “The Liberal Order Framework: A Prospectus for a Reconnaissance of Canadian History” (2000). Later readings: Rebels, Reds, Radicals (2005); Reasoning Otherwise (2008); “Canada as a Long Liberal Revolution” (2009).
nodes.scope_note: This entry presents the 1992 article and the 1994 book on antimodernism and the folk, and the two essays of 2000 on region and liberal order. The 1992 article is read at pp. 5–9 and 13–14; the 1994 book is checked at summary and contents level, with its closing argument (p. 306) quoted by Muise (1998); the region essay is read in full; the prospectus is checked at abstract level, with pp. 620–21 quoted by Fecteau (2009). The framework takes its name from his prospectus, but state-formation studies (Curtis 1988; Greer and Radforth 1992) precede it and commentators name Gramsci and Fernande Roy (1988) as its sources; he is not presented as the founder of a field. The 2005, 2008 and 2009 works are later readings.

nodes.label: Harold A. Innis
nodes.date_label: The Fur Trade in Canada 1930 · The Cod Fisheries 1940 · Empire and Communications 1950 · The Bias of Communication 1951 · coverage through 2000
nodes.description: A Toronto political economist whose staple studies read Canada's development through the export of raw materials to industrial centres in Britain and the United States. The Fur Trade in Canada (1930) concludes that 'the economic history of Canada has been dominated by the discrepancy between the center and the margin of western civilization', that the history of the fur trade is 'the history of contact between two civilizations', and that 'the present Dominion emerged not in spite of geography but because of it'. The Cod Fisheries (1940) follows a second staple as the history of an international economy. After 1940 he turned to the media of communication and empire (Empire and Communications, 1950; The Bias of Communication, 1951).
nodes.representative_figures_and_works: Harold A. Innis (1894–1952); The Fur Trade in Canada: An Introduction to Canadian Economic History (1930); The Cod Fisheries: The History of an International Economy (1940); Empire and Communications (1950); The Bias of Communication (1951; 1964 reissue with an introduction by Marshall McLuhan). Readings: Brady's memoir (1953); Watkins, “A Staple Theory of Economic Growth” (1963); Salmon (1997).
nodes.scope_note: This entry presents the staple studies. The Fur Trade in Canada is checked at its contents and its conclusion (pp. 386–397, read in a scan of the 1930 edition); The Cod Fisheries and the two communication books are checked at catalogue level, and the turn to communication rests on Brady's 1953 memoir. He is not presented as the originator of the staple approach. Watkins (1963) calls him its 'leading innovator' but adds that 'others tilled the same vineyard'. Salmon (1997) notes that 'Innis never claimed to have originated the staples theory', Brady names Adam Shortt 'the pioneer in these economic studies', and Mackintosh's 1923 article precedes the fur-trade book. The 1930 conclusion's statements about Indigenous peoples (their 'limited cultural background'; that Canada 'has had no serious problems with her native peoples') are recorded as claims of 1930, not adopted. The atlas has no communication-studies entry; the McLuhan introduction is noted from the catalogue only.

edges.relationship: Canadian new labour historians draw on Thompson's class and culture, and critics contest whether it fits Canada
edges.evidence_note: Both sides of the 1981 Labour/Le Travailleur exchange, read in full, treat Thompson as the reference point for Canadian new labour history. Kealey (pp. 82–83) calls The Making 'probably the most influential piece of historical writing in the English language published since 1960' and says 'Thompson's influence is our concern'. In North America, critics attack 'works which have associated themselves with Thompson's method'. He concedes (p. 87) that users of British social history must show that it applies 'to the Canadian context'. Bercuson (pp. 97–98) says Canadian new labour historians 'follow the thinking of E.P. Thompson' and 'lean to the British experience', studying culture 'in the Thompson sense'. Palmer, he says, echoes Thompson. Bercuson objects (p. 108) that 'even if Thompson is right about England, his concepts do not necessarily apply anywhere else'. McNaught's 1981 CHR title frames the decade as 'E. P. Thompson vs Harold Logan'. Palmer, a leading new labour historian, wrote a book on Thompson (1981). Limits: this is testimony from the debate about Thompson's influence, not a reading of Palmer's or Kealey's monographs. Gutman is named alongside Thompson throughout, and the claim is about a resource and reference point, not adoption of one theory. PhD context: 38 of 106 Canadian History PhDs (2009–2026) citing Thompson engage this field (36%, lift 1.64).
edges.map_label: Thompson and Canadian new labour history

edges.relationship: Scott's theory of gender is weighed in Canadian debates over discourse, experience and gender history
edges.evidence_note: Valverde's 1990 review essay in Labour/Le Travail, read in full, treats Scott's Gender and the Politics of History (with Riley) as a key work in 'the controversy about discourse theory'. She notes that poststructuralism had a 'bad reputation … among socialists and feminists (in English Canada, at least)' and that 'in Canada' the debate was posed as 'a yes-or-no question'. She concludes that Scott 'deserves to be carefully read even by those who find some of its more polemical claims hard to swallow'. Pierson's 1991 essay on Canadian women's history opens on the turn to deconstruction, with Scott's theorising of gender as its most acclaimed example (opening read). Reference lists show Scott cited by Linda Kealey (1992), Pierson (1992) and Parr's 1995 CHR essay on gender history (OpenAlex metadata; texts unread). Limits: the evidence shows engagement and debate, not adoption. Valverde is sympathetic but critical. Palmer's Descent into Discourse (1990) is a Canadian critique of the linguistic turn, but its treatment of Scott was not checked here. The 1995–96 Left History exchange is title-level and is not evidence that names Scott. PhD context: 64 of 120 Canadian History PhDs citing Scott engage this field (53%, lift 2.12); 39 engage childhood and youth (lift 3.21), and 49 working-class history (lift 1.87).
edges.map_label: Scott's gender theory in Canadian debates

edges.relationship: Settler colonialism as the frame for a history of anthropology (1999)
edges.evidence_note: The 1999 book names settler colonialism in its title. Its contents page titles the introduction 'Text and Context: Anthropology and Settler Colonialism' and chapter 1 'White Man's Flour: Virgin Birth in Anthropology and in Australian Settler Discourse'; chapter 2 is 'Science, Colonialism and Anthropology: The Logic of a Global Transformation'. Library subject headings add Australian frontier life, imperialism and racism in anthropology. Introduction pp. 1–2 read: settler colonies 'were (are) premised on the elimination of native societies' and 'invasion is a structure not an event'. The rest of the book is checked at contents and catalogue level. A contribution, not a founding: earlier settler-society studies (1983, 1995) and earlier usage of the term (Veracini 2013) precede it. In the sampled corpus, 17 of 1,303 strict History doctoral dissertations dated 2009–2026 cite the book (earliest observed citation 2012) and 54 cite any of his works; the citation share rises from 1.0% (2009–14) to 8.6% (2020–26). Bibliographies record consultation, not influence. The 2006 essay is a later reading, not evidence for this edge.

edges.relationship: A history of Victorian and Australian anthropology in its settler-colonial setting
edges.evidence_note: In-period evidence (1999). The contents page lists chapters on mother-right ('Sex and Property in Victorian Anthropology'), totemism ('Victorian Anthropology's Eternal Dichotomy') and E. B. Tylor ('Survival in a Paradigm Shift: E.B. Tylor and the Problem of the Text'), alongside virgin birth in anthropology and in Australian settler discourse. Catalogue subjects: Anthropology -- Australia -- History; Racism in anthropology -- Australia. Introduction p. 1 read: the book is 'a history not so much of anthropology itself as of its ideological entanglements'. The chapters' stance toward these anthropologists is not read here. If the introduction confirms a critical argument, a critique edge to anthropology/evolution may be the better reading. A historian's account of the discipline, not anthropological fieldwork.

edges.relationship: Canada as a project of liberal rule: the prospectus of 2000
edges.evidence_note: In-period evidence (2000). The prospectus abstract (read) proposes mapping 'the Canadian state as a project of liberal rule in northern North America' to get beyond the 'socio-cultural versus national-political impasse'. Its core formulation (pp. 620–21) is checked as quoted by Fecteau (2009): 'Canada-as-project can be analyzed through the study of the implantation and expansion over a heterogeneous terrain of a certain politico-economic logic – to wit liberalism.' The prospectus body is not read here. McKay's spring 2000 Acadiensis essay (pp. 90–91, read) sets out the same programme in his own words: 'a strategy of reconnaissance'; the project 'was the project of liberal order, a coherent attempt to install a liberal public philosophy and practice of "peace, order and good government" in northern North America'; 'Canada was thus a process, not a self-evident thing, and the key to this process was liberalization'. A contribution, not a founding: state-formation studies (Curtis 1988; Greer and Radforth 1992) precede it, and Pâquet (2009) names Gramsci and Fernande Roy (1988) as its sources. In the sampled corpus, 90 of 1,303 strict History doctoral dissertations dated 2009–2026 cite the prospectus. Bibliographies record consultation, not influence. The 2009 reply and the histories of the left (2005, 2008) are later readings, not evidence for this edge.

edges.relationship: Antimodernism and the invented folk in twentieth-century Nova Scotia (1992, 1994)
edges.evidence_note: In-period evidence (1992, 1994). In 'Tartanism Triumphant' (Acadiensis, 1992; pp. 5–9 read) McKay asks how Nova Scotia 'became Scottish' in the second quarter of the twentieth century, when 'a collection of hazy generalizations and ethnic stereotypes' became 'a natural and obvious "commonsense"'. His broad answer: 'it was part of an international anti-modernist wave, a local version of a general middle-class search for something outside and better than the crisis-ridden modern world it inhabited' (pp. 8–9); the narrow answer is the state's cultural power under Angus L. Macdonald. Note 12 takes Lears's definition of American antimodernism and adds the 'simple life' and 'nature'. The Quest of the Folk (1994) is checked at summary and contents level: chapters on 'The Idea of the Folk', Helen Creighton and folklore, Mary Black and handicrafts, the simple life, and the folk 'under conditions of postmodernity'. Muise's review essay (Acadiensis, 1998; pp. 128–32 read) describes the three case studies and quotes the book's conclusion that 'the concept of the Folk was and remains a powerful obstacle to the formation of a counter-hegemonic cultural politics' (p. 306). Wright's 1995 Acadiensis review essay on English-Canadian intellectual history cites the book for 'a very skilled handling of Antonio Gramsci's theory of cultural hegemony by an historian' (p. 132 n. 29). A contribution to the field's cultural strand, not its origin: Berger, McKillop and Owram precede it. In the sampled corpus, 56 of 1,303 strict History doctoral dissertations dated 2009–2026 cite the book. Bibliographies record consultation, not influence. In the Province of History (2010, with Bates) is a later reading.

edges.relationship: Rethinking 'region' inside a history of the liberal project (2000)
edges.evidence_note: In-period evidence (Acadiensis, spring 2000; pp. 89–101 read; a lightly edited version of a talk prepared for the August 1997 Atlantic Canada Workshop, dated here by publication). McKay finds that the 1990s 'multiplication of subject-positions, epistemologies and methodologies places a question mark over the very concept of an "Atlantic Canada"' (p. 90). He then asks where region fits a history of Canada as a liberal project and answers 'Quite centrally' (p. 95). He sets aside natural, essentialist definitions of the region (pp. 95–96); he finds heartland–hinterland and dependency models descriptively rich, but asks them to 'undergo the rigorous analysis of concepts' (pp. 96–99). He would resist a nationalizing historiography that reduces the region to one inferior term (p. 99). As an agenda he proposes exploring 'the remarkable extent to which Atlantic Canadians built the Canadian liberal project' (p. 99) and a regional 'communitarian critique of the liberal order' (p. 100). He also rejects the charge that regionalists are a 'balkanizing faction' (p. 91). This is a reconsideration from inside the field. In the sampled corpus, 4 of 1,303 strict History doctoral dissertations dated 2009–2026 cite the essay under its main record (one more under a variant record).

edges.relationship: The staple studies: Canada read through its exports of fur and fish (1930, 1940)
edges.evidence_note: Innis's own statement, 1930 conclusion (pp. 386–397 read): 'The economic history of Canada has been dominated by the discrepancy between the center and the margin of western civilization. Energy has been directed toward the exploitation of staple products and the tendency has been cumulative' (p. 388); 'The northern half of North America remained British because of the importance of fur as a staple product' (p. 396); 'The present Dominion emerged not in spite of geography but because of it' (p. 397). Watkins (1963, opening paragraphs read) calls him 'the leading innovator' whose work 'stamped the “school”', with an approach 'more technological history writ large than a theory of economic growth'. Brady (1953, read in full) traces his study of 'the staple industries, beginning with the fur trade and fisheries' (p. 89). Salmon (1997, pp. 180–181 read): the staple thesis 'provided an economic rationale for Canadian political development'. A contribution, not a founding: Watkins says 'others tilled the same vineyard', Salmon notes that 'Innis never claimed to have originated the staples theory' (n. 2), Brady calls Adam Shortt 'the pioneer in these economic studies' (p. 91), and Mackintosh's 1923 article precedes the book. The Cod Fisheries is checked at catalogue level only. In the sampled corpus, 82 of 1,303 strict History doctoral dissertations dated 2009–2026 cite any of his works; the citation share falls from 7.1% (2009–14) and 6.8% (2015–19) to 4.9% (2020–26). Of the 82, 48 cite The Fur Trade in Canada and 6 The Cod Fisheries. Bibliographies record consultation, not influence.

sources.title: Alexander Brady, "Harold Adams Innis, 1894–1952," Canadian Journal of Economics and Political Science 19, no. 1 (1953): 87–96.
sources.citation: Alexander Brady, "Harold Adams Innis, 1894–1952," Canadian Journal of Economics and Political Science 19, no. 1 (February 1953): 87–96.

verification.note: Read in full (Cambridge Core PDF; Crossref: CJEPS 19:1, Feb. 1953, pp. 87–96). Born 5 November 1894 near Otterville, died 8 November 1952 (p. 87); Veblen, Clark and Duncan as Chicago influences (pp. 88–89); study of 'the staple industries, beginning with the fur trade and fisheries' (p. 89); The Fur Trade in Canada as 'his first notable achievement in economic interpretation', with themes including 'the relation between the culture of the Indian and the spread of European power' and 'the adaptation of the Indian to the needs of the trade'; 'modern Canada had emerged, not in spite of geography, but because of it'; it 'established the reputation of its author as one of the leading economic historians in North America' (p. 90); 'Adam Shortt, as Innis would promptly admit, was the pioneer in these economic studies' (p. 91); 'after 1940 he became increasingly absorbed by the wider themes of cultural history' and 'more keenly interested in the media of communication' (pp. 91–92); Empire and Communications (1950; the 1948 Beit Lectures) 'served a purpose in setting forth a theme for future social scientists to pursue' (pp. 94–95); president of the Economic History Association, 1942 (p. 95). A colleague's memorial, not a critical assessment.

sources.scope_note: In-period memoir: the staple studies, the turn to communication, and Shortt as the earlier pioneer.

sources.title: Ian McKay, “Tartanism Triumphant: The Construction of Scottishness in Nova Scotia, 1933–1954,” Acadiensis 21, no. 2 (Spring 1992): 5–47.
sources.citation: Ian McKay, “Tartanism Triumphant: The Construction of Scottishness in Nova Scotia, 1933–1954,” Acadiensis 21, no. 2 (Spring 1992): 5–47.

verification.note: PDF citation line on p. 5: Acadiensis XXI, 2 (Spring 1992), pp. 5–47; author line Ian McKay. Pages 5–9 read closely, with notes 1–13. Nova Scotia 'became Scottish' in the second quarter of the twentieth century; 'hazy generalizations and ethnic stereotypes' became 'a natural and obvious "commonsense"'. Broad answer: 'it was part of an international anti-modernist wave, a local version of a general middle-class search for something outside and better than the crisis-ridden modern world it inhabited' (pp. 8–9). Narrow answer: Premier Angus L. Macdonald 'used the state's cultural power' to fuse a romantic, essentialist Scottishness with tourism (p. 9). Note 12 (p. 9) quotes Lears's definition of American antimodernism (No Place of Grace, p. xv) and adds 'and, I would also add, in the "simple life" and in "nature"'. Pages 13–14 and note 32 also read: the concept of 'invented tradition' is useful 'provided it is acknowledged that all traditions are historically constructed', and Trevor-Roper is said to rely on 'a naive historical realism'. Note 1: a revised version of a paper given to the CHA in 1990. The rest of the article was searched by keyword only, not read. Checked against: UNB Libraries Acadiensis article page and PDF (article/view/11913; PDF download 11913/12757).

sources.scope_note: McKay's own in-period statement of antimodernism as the frame for Nova Scotia's invented identity; his checked use of Lears.

sources.citation: D. A. Muise, “Who Owns History Anyway? Reinventing Atlantic Canada for Pleasure and Profit,” Acadiensis 27, no. 2 (Spring 1998): 124–34.

verification.note: Review essay; PDF citation line on p. 124 and signature 'D. A. MUISE'. Pages 124 and 128–32 read (the section on The Quest of the Folk). Muise writes that the book 'examines the origins of the essentialist folk tradition' and that McKay 'explodes the central place of the "folk" in understanding Nova Scotia's culture and history'. He describes three case studies (Helen Creighton, Mary Black and handicrafts, and literary producers including the Song Fishermen) and an afterword, 'The Folk under Conditions of Postmodernity'. McKay acknowledges a debt to Whisnant and Raymond Williams and places himself 'within a neo-marxist framework associated with the work of Antonio Gramsci'. Muise quotes the book (p. 306): 'the concept of the Folk was and remains a powerful obstacle to the formation of a counter-hegemonic cultural politics, without which a new, profoundly emancipatory politics of class, gender and racial equality is inconceivable.' Note 9 lists McKay's earlier essays on the theme (1988, 1992, 1993). Pages 125–27 not read; pp. 133–34 only glanced at (to the signature). Checked against: UNB Libraries Acadiensis article page and PDF (article/view/10846; PDF 10846/11670).

verification.note: Érudit PDFs (llt32ob01, llt33art01) opened; Érudit citation gives pp. 10–72 and 13–68; Crossref record for Part II (doi:10.2307/25143788). Read: Part I opening, p. 10: Thompson's histories “occupy a special and influential place”, alongside “a nagging denigration of his accomplishments”; a footnote lists Greg Kealey's obituary in the St. John's Evening Telegram (5 September 1993). Keyword search of both parts found biography and political history, not an account of Thompson's reception in Canadian labour history (except Queen's University seminars in 1988 and a Kingston theatre visit). Shows that the Canadian Committee on Labour History's journal gave Thompson a two-part obituary of some 120 pages; it is not evidence of his influence on Canadian research.

verification.note: Full text read (Érudit PDF, Review Essays, pp. 227–236); Crossref and OpenAlex records (OpenAlex abstract = opening paragraphs). p. 227: reviews Riley and Scott as “two key works” in “the controversy about discourse theory”; “Some of Joan Scott's essays are biting attacks on empiricism, particularly as practiced by historians of women”; ‘experience’ was “the central category in the pioneering work of E.P. Thompson”. p. 228: poststructuralism's “bad reputation … among socialists and feminists (in English Canada, at least)”. p. 233: “Scott's work deserves to be carefully read even by those who find some of its more polemical claims hard to swallow”; she may exaggerate what Foucault and Derrida can contribute and in “her reaction against both Thompsonian and empiricist traditions”. Note on p. 233: “In Canada, the debate about theory and discourse, such as it is, seems to be posed as a yes-or-no question”. Valverde (York University) writes as a participant; this is a sympathetic but critical review, not a survey of Canadian practice.

wcreq_kealey_1981.note: Pages 67–68 and 82–87 read closely with their footnotes; the rest skimmed by keyword (Érudit PDF, id.erudit.org/iderudit/llt7cri01; Critiques section, pp. 67–94, which also confirms the end page the existing record inferred). p. 67: the moment for evaluating the labour history of the 1960s–70s has arrived, signalled in Britain by the confrontation of “Althusserian structuralism and Thompsonian ‘culturalist’ or ‘socialist-humanist’ history”. p. 68: names McNaught’s forthcoming “E.P. Thompson vs. Harold Logan” as making “only too clear the eminently political nature of the emerging debate”. pp. 82–83: The Making of the English Working Class “has probably been the most influential piece of historical writing in the English language published since 1960”; “For our purposes, Thompson’s influence is our concern”; in North America “the critics are most often anti-Marxists attacking works which have associated themselves with Thompson’s method”. p. 87: quotes Bercuson (1979) accusing working-class historians of paying “due obeisance to E.P. Thompson, the guru” and “shoehorning their subjects into a Thompsonian mould”, and concedes that those “who utilize the insights of British … social history” must “demonstrate convincingly that they apply to the Canadian context”. The footnotes to these pages were read; the rest of the essay was skimmed by keyword only.

wcreq_bercuson_1981.note: Full text read (Érudit PDF, id.erudit.org/iderudit/llt7cri02, pp. 95–112). p. 97: Canadian practitioners of the new labour history “follow the thinking of E.P. Thompson in Britain, Herbert Gutman in the United States, and others in applying the culturalist approach to Canadian experience”; “Palmer, echoing E.P. Thompson, regards culture and conflict as ‘complementary processes’” (citing A Culture in Conflict, p. xii, which was not itself checked). p. 98: in Canada new labour historians “stand in the middle but so far tend to lean to the British experience. They study working-class culture for the explanation and definition they believe it offers in the Thompson sense”. p. 108: “Even if Thompson is right about England, his concepts do not necessarily apply anywhere else.” A critic’s characterization, not a self-description.

cdnsrc_parr_1995.note: OpenAlex reference list for the article (W2118812311; 33 matched references) includes three works by Scott: 'The Evidence of Experience' (1991), 'Deconstructing Equality-versus-Difference' and 'The Campaign against Political Correctness' (1992), alongside Riley, Canning and Sonya Rose on gender history and women's history. Reference-matching metadata only; how Parr uses them was not read.

cdng_mckay_2000_region.note: the whole essay (pp. 89–101) read in the UNB PDF. Note 1 (p. 89): 'a lightly-edited version of the introductory talk I prepared for the Atlantic Canada Workshop which met in Halifax in August 1997'. Pages 90–91 state the liberal-order programme: 'a strategy of reconnaissance'; 'That project, very briefly, was the project of liberal order, a coherent attempt to install a liberal public philosophy and practice of "peace, order and good government" in northern North America'; 'Canada was thus a process, not a self-evident thing, and the key to this process was liberalization'. Where region fits that approach: 'Quite centrally' (p. 95). The essay sets aside natural and essentialist definitions (pp. 95–96), asks heartland–hinterland and dependency models to 'undergo the rigorous analysis of concepts' (pp. 96–99) and resists a nationalizing historiography (p. 99). It proposes exploring 'the remarkable extent to which Atlantic Canadians built the Canadian liberal project' (p. 99) and the region's 'communitarian critique of the liberal order' (p. 100). Page 89 names 'the Gramscian assumptions that have shaped my outlook'.

edge_886.relationship: Marxist class analysis in Canadian labour history
edge_886.evidence_note: Kealey’s 1981 essay strongly defends class analysis and the study of working-class culture, and McNaught’s 1981 critique answers the new labour history. A contribution of Marxist class analysis as a resource to the ‘new labour history: class, culture and community’ strand; no claim that Canadian historians adopted one Marxist theory. Thompson’s own place is the separate edge from his person entry (revision 1.129).

deferred_relationships.reason: There is no checked pre-2000 passage in which a Canadian women's or gender historian engages Family Fortunes or Hall. The available pre-2000 items are metadata-level reviews and one family-history abstract whose citation of Family Fortunes is visible only in its reference list. The edge as drafted (an undirected comparison) is for a later extension release once Parr's 1993 review, Morgan's 1996 introduction or 1998 review, or a 1990s separate-spheres article is read. A contribution supported only by post-2000 publications (e.g. Perry 2001; Hall 2002; Christie, ed., Households of Faith, 2002) requires the extension workflow; a checked 1990s passage could support an ordinary in-period edge.
